prompt:
Let $f:[0,1]\to(0,\infty)$ be an integrable function such that $f(x)\cdot f(1-x)=1$ for all $x\in[0,1]$. Prove that
$$\int_0^1f(x)\,dx\ge1 .$$

solutions.title: AM-GM on symmetric pairs
solutions.body:
For every $x\in[0,1]$, by the AM-GM inequality and the hypothesis,
$$f(x)+f(1-x)\ge2\sqrt{f(x)f(1-x)}=2 .$$
Split the integral at $\frac12$ and substitute $x\mapsto1-x$ in the second half:
$$\int_0^1f(x)\,dx=\int_0^{1/2}f(x)\,dx+\int_{1/2}^1f(x)\,dx=\int_0^{1/2}\big(f(x)+f(1-x)\big)\,dx\ge\int_0^{1/2}2\,dx=1 .$$
∎

solutions.title: Cauchy–Schwarz
solutions.body:
Let $I=\int_0^1f(x)\,dx>0$. Substituting $x\mapsto1-x$ and using $f(1-x)=1/f(x)$,
$$I=\int_0^1f(1-x)\,dx=\int_0^1\frac{dx}{f(x)} .$$
(In particular $1/f$ is integrable.) By the Cauchy–Schwarz inequality,
$$I^2=\int_0^1f(x)\,dx\cdot\int_0^1\frac{dx}{f(x)}\ge\left(\int_0^1\sqrt{f(x)}\cdot\frac1{\sqrt{f(x)}}\,dx\right)^2=1 .$$
Since $I>0$, $I\ge1$. ∎

answer: Only $A=0$. Transposing gives $A^k\big(I+(I+A^{k-1})^k\big)=0$, whose polynomial has $0$ as its only real root; so $A$ is nilpotent, $A^k=0$, $A=A^T$ is symmetric nilpotent, hence $0$.

solutions.title: An annihilating polynomial
solutions.body:
**Answer: only the zero matrix.** Clearly $A=0$ works.

Conversely, let $A$ satisfy $A^T=A+A^k$ with $k\ge n$. Transposing, $A=A^T+(A^T)^k$, and substituting $A^T=A+A^k$:
$$A=A+A^k+(A+A^k)^k\quad\Longrightarrow\quad A^k+\big(A(I+A^{k-1})\big)^k=0 .$$
The factors $A$ and $I+A^{k-1}$ commute, so this reads
$$A^k\Big(I+\big(I+A^{k-1}\big)^k\Big)=0 .$$
Thus $p(x)=x^k\big(1+(1+x^{k-1})^k\big)$ annihilates $A$. If $\lambda$ is an eigenvalue with eigenvector $v\ne0$, then $0=p(A)v=p(\lambda)v$, so $p(\lambda)=0$.

All eigenvalues of $A$ are real, and for real $x$ the second factor of $p$ is positive: if $k$ is even, $(1+x^{k-1})^k\ge0$; if $k$ is odd, $k-1$ is even, so $1+x^{k-1}\ge1$. Hence every eigenvalue is $0$.

So the characteristic polynomial of $A$ is $x^n$, and by Cayley–Hamilton $A^n=0$; as $k\ge n$, $A^k=0$ and therefore $A^T=A$. A real symmetric matrix is orthogonally diagonalisable, $A=QDQ^T$, and $D$ has the eigenvalues (all $0$) on its diagonal, so $A=0$. ∎

solutions.title: Eigenvalues map to eigenvalues
solutions.body:
$A=0$ works; let $A$ be any solution with $k\ge n$.

If $\lambda$ is a (real) eigenvalue of $A$ with real eigenvector $v$, then $A^Tv=Av+A^kv=(\lambda+\lambda^k)v$, so $\lambda+\lambda^k$ is an eigenvalue of $A^T$, hence of $A$ (same characteristic polynomial).

* **$k$ odd.** Take an eigenvalue $\lambda$ of largest absolute value. If $\lambda\ne0$, then $|\lambda+\lambda^k|=|\lambda|\,(1+\lambda^{k-1})>|\lambda|$ (as $k-1$ is even), contradicting maximality. So all eigenvalues are $0$.
* **$k$ even.** Taking traces in $A^T=A+A^k$ gives $\operatorname{tr}A^k=0$, i.e. $\sum\lambda_i^k=0$ over the (real) eigenvalues with multiplicity. Each term is $\ge0$ as $k$ is even, so all $\lambda_i=0$.

Hence $A$ is nilpotent, $A^n=0$ (Cayley–Hamilton), so $A^k=0$ and $A=A^T$. A symmetric matrix with all eigenvalues $0$ is $0$ (it is orthogonally diagonalisable). **Answer: $A=0$.** ∎

prompt: Let $p$ be a prime number. A flea is staying at point $0$ of the real line. At each minute, the flea has three possibilities: to stay at its position, or to move by $1$ to the left or to the right. After $p-1$ minutes, it wants to be at $0$ again. Denote by $f(p)$ the number of its strategies to do this (for example, $f(3)=3$: it may either stay at $0$ for the entire time, or go to the left and then to the right, or go to the right and then to the left). Find $f(p)$ modulo $p$.

solutions.title: Generating function over $\mathbb F_p$
solutions.body:
**Answer:** modulo $p$, $f(p)\equiv0$ for $p=3$, $f(p)\equiv1$ for $p\equiv1\pmod3$, and $f(p)\equiv-1$ for $p\equiv2\pmod3$.

A strategy is a sequence of $p-1$ moves from $\{-1,0,+1\}$ with sum $0$. Encoding the moves by $x^{-1},1,x$, $f(p)$ is the constant term of $(x^{-1}+1+x)^{p-1}$, i.e.
$$f(p)=[x^{p-1}]\,(1+x+x^2)^{p-1}.$$
Work with formal power series with coefficients in $\mathbb F_p$. Since $1+x+x^2=\frac{1-x^3}{1-x}$,
$$(1+x+x^2)^{p-1}=\frac{(1-x^3)^{p}}{1-x^3}\cdot\frac{1-x}{(1-x)^{p}}=\frac{(1-x^{3p})(1-x)}{(1-x^3)(1-x^p)},$$
using $(1-y)^p=1-y^p$ in characteristic $p$. Modulo $x^p$ we have $1-x^{3p}\equiv1$ and $\frac1{1-x^p}\equiv1$, and we only need the coefficient of $x^{p-1}$. Hence
$$f(p)\equiv[x^{p-1}]\,\frac{1-x}{1-x^3}=[x^{p-1}]\,(1-x)\sum_{j\ge0}x^{3j}=c(p-1)-c(p-2)\pmod p,$$
where $c(i)=1$ if $3\mid i$ and $0$ otherwise.

* $p\equiv1\pmod3$: $c(p-1)-c(p-2)=1-0=1$.
* $p\equiv2\pmod3$ (including $p=2$): $0-1=-1$.
* $p=3$: $c(2)-c(1)=0$ (indeed $f(3)=3\equiv0$).

∎

solutions.title: Cyclic shifts and a linear system
solutions.body:
($p=2$: the only strategy is to stay, $f(2)=1\equiv-1\pmod2$; $p=3$: $f(3)=3\equiv0$. Let $p\ge5$.)

For a residue $i$ mod $p$ and $t\ge0$ let $a_i(t)$ be the number of $t$-move strategies ending at a position $\equiv i\pmod p$. After $p-1$ moves the position lies in $[-(p-1),p-1]$, so it is $\equiv0$ only if it is $0$: $f(p)=a_0(p-1)$. Also $a_i(t+1)=a_{i-1}(t)+a_i(t)+a_{i+1}(t)$ (indices mod $p$), according to the last move.

**Strategies of length $p$.** The cyclic group $\mathbb Z/p$ acts on sequences of $p$ moves by rotation, preserving the sum. A non-constant sequence has an orbit of size exactly $p$ (the stabiliser is a proper subgroup of a group of prime order). The three constant sequences all end at a position $\equiv0$ ($0$, $p$, $-p$). Hence $a_0(p)\equiv3$ and $a_i(p)\equiv0$ for $i\ne0$, modulo $p$.

So $x_i=a_i(p-1)$ satisfies, modulo $p$,
$$x_{i-1}+x_i+x_{i+1}\equiv3\delta_{i,0}\qquad(i\in\mathbb Z/p).$$
**Uniqueness.** Let $S$ be the cyclic shift on $\mathbb F_p^{\,p}$. Then $S^p=I$, so $(S-I)^p=S^p-I=0$ (characteristic $p$): $S=I+N$ with $N$ nilpotent. Since $S^{-1}=(I+N)^{-1}=I-N+N^2-\dots$, the system matrix is $S^{-1}+I+S=3I+N'$, where $N'$ is a polynomial in $N$ without constant term and hence nilpotent; so it is invertible because $3\ne0$ in $\mathbb F_p$. So the system has exactly one solution mod $p$.

**The solution.** If $p=3m+1$, take $x_i=1$ for $i\equiv0,1\pmod3$ and $x_i=-2$ for $i\equiv2\pmod 3$ ($0\le i\le p-1$). Any three cyclically consecutive entries inside $0..p-1$ sum to $0$; at the wrap-around, $x_{p-1}+x_0+x_1=1+1+1=3$ and $x_{p-2}+x_{p-1}+x_0=-2+1+1=0$. So this is the solution and $f(p)\equiv x_0=1$.

If $p=3m+2$, take $x_i=-1,2,-1$ for $i\equiv0,1,2\pmod3$. Interior triples sum to $0$; $x_{p-1}+x_0+x_1=2-1+2=3$ and $x_{p-2}+x_{p-1}+x_0=-1+2-1=0$. So $f(p)\equiv x_0=-1$.

**Answer:** $f(p)\equiv1$ if $p\equiv1\pmod3$, $f(p)\equiv-1$ if $p\equiv2\pmod 3$, $f(3)\equiv0$. ∎

prompt:
Let $n>3$ be an integer. Let $\Omega$ be the set of all triples of distinct elements of $\{1,2,\dots,n\}$. Let $m$ denote the minimal number of colours which suffice to colour $\Omega$ so that whenever $1\le a<b<c<d\le n$, the triples $\{a,b,c\}$ and $\{b,c,d\}$ have different colours. Prove that
$$\frac1{100}\log\log n\le m\le100\log\log n .$$
answer: Shift graphs: with $G_k$ the digraph on $k$-subsets ($\{a_1<\dots<a_k\}\to\{a_2<\dots<a_{k+1}\}$), $\chi(G_k)=b(G_{k-1})$ where $b$ is the least number of "no directed 2-path" edge classes, and $\log_2\chi(G)\le b(G)\le2\lceil\log_2\chi(G)\rceil$. Since $\chi(G_1)=n$, $\log_2\log_2n\le m=\chi(G_3)\le2\lceil\log_2\lceil\log_2n\rceil\rceil$.

solutions.title: Shift graphs and binary colourings
solutions.body:
Here $\log$ is the natural logarithm. We prove the sharper bounds
$$\log_2\log_2n\ \le\ m\ \le\ 2\big\lceil\log_2\lceil\log_2n\rceil\big\rceil .\tag{$*$}$$

**Shift graphs.** For $k\ge1$ let $G_k$ be the directed graph whose vertices are the $k$-subsets of $[n]=\{1,\dots,n\}$, with an edge $\{a_1,\dots,a_k\}\to\{a_2,\dots,a_{k+1}\}$ for each $(k+1)$-subset $a_1<\dots<a_{k+1}$. Edges of $G_k$ are thus in bijection with $(k+1)$-subsets. The required colourings of $\Omega$ are exactly the proper vertex colourings of $G_3$, so $m=\chi(G_3)$.

Call a set $E_1$ of edges of a digraph **admissible** if it contains no directed path $u\to v\to w$ of two edges, and let $b(G)$ be the minimum number of admissible sets covering all edges.

**Lemma 1.** A set of $k$-subsets is independent in $G_k$ iff, as a set of edges of $G_{k-1}$, it is admissible. Hence $\chi(G_k)=b(G_{k-1})$ for $k\ge2$.

*Proof.* A directed 2-path in $G_{k-1}$ is $\{a_1..a_{k-1}\}\to\{a_2..a_k\}\to\{a_3..a_{k+1}\}$ for some $a_1<\dots<a_{k+1}$; its two edges are the $k$-sets $\{a_1..a_k\}$ and $\{a_2..a_{k+1}\}$, which are exactly the endpoints of an edge of $G_k$, and every edge of $G_k$ arises this way. So "no 2-path inside the set" is the same as "no edge inside the set". Covering by independent sets is the same as colouring (subsets of independent/admissible sets stay so), so $\chi(G_k)=b(G_{k-1})$. $\square$

**Lemma 2.** For every digraph $G$ without loops, $\log_2\chi(G)\le b(G)\le2\lceil\log_2\chi(G)\rceil$.

*Proof.* (Lower bound.) Let $E_1,\dots,E_b$ be admissible sets covering the edges. Colour each vertex $v$ by the set $c(v)=\{i:\ v\text{ has an outgoing edge in }E_i\}\subseteq[b]$. For an edge $v\to w$, pick $i$ with $v\to w\in E_i$; then $i\in c(v)$, and $i\notin c(w)$, since an edge $w\to u$ in $E_i$ would form a 2-path $v\to w\to u$ in $E_i$. So $c(v)\ne c(w)$, $c$ is a proper colouring with at most $2^b$ colours, and $\chi(G)\le2^{b}$.

(Upper bound.) Let $\chi(G)=q$, $\tau:V\to\{0,\dots,q-1\}$ a proper colouring and $r=\lceil\log_2q\rceil$, so every colour has an $r$-bit binary expansion; let $\varepsilon_i(x)$ be bit $i$ of $x$. For $i=0,\dots,r-1$ set
$$E_{i,+}=\{v\to u:\ \varepsilon_i(\tau(v))=0,\ \varepsilon_i(\tau(u))=1\},\qquad E_{i,-}=\{v\to u:\ \varepsilon_i(\tau(v))=1,\ \varepsilon_i(\tau(u))=0\}.$$
A 2-path $v\to w\to u$ inside $E_{i,+}$ would need bit $i$ of $\tau(w)$ to be both $1$ and $0$; so each set is admissible (same for $E_{i,-}$). Every edge $v\to u$ has $\tau(v)\ne\tau(u)$, so they differ in some bit $i$ and the edge lies in $E_{i,+}$ or $E_{i,-}$. Thus $b(G)\le2r$. $\square$

**Putting it together.** $G_1$ has vertices $1,\dots,n$ and an edge $i\to j$ for all $i<j$, so $\chi(G_1)=n$. Moreover $b(G_1)\le\lceil\log_2n\rceil$: with $\tau(v)=v-1$, for $v<u$ the highest bit where $v-1$ and $u-1$ differ is $0$ in $v-1$ and $1$ in $u-1$, so the $\lceil\log_2 n\rceil$ sets $E_{i,+}$ already cover all edges. Using Lemmas 1 and 2:
$$\chi(G_2)=b(G_1)\in\big[\log_2n,\ \lceil\log_2n\rceil\big],$$
$$m=\chi(G_3)=b(G_2)\ \ge\ \log_2\chi(G_2)\ \ge\ \log_2\log_2n,\qquad m=b(G_2)\le2\lceil\log_2\chi(G_2)\rceil\le2\big\lceil\log_2\lceil\log_2n\rceil\big\rceil .$$
This is $(*)$.

**The stated bounds.** Let $L=\log\log n$; for $n\ge4$, $L\ge\log\log4>0.32$. Since $\log_2\log_2n=\frac{L-\log\log2}{\log2}=\frac{L+0.366\ldots}{0.693\ldots}\ge L$, the lower bound gives $m\ge L\ge\frac{L}{100}$. For the upper bound, $\lceil\log_2n\rceil\le2\log_2n$ and $\lceil y\rceil\le y+1$, so
$$m\le2\big(\log_2(2\log_2n)+1\big)=4+2\log_2\log_2n\le4+2\cdot\frac{L+0.37}{0.69}<5.1+2.9L .$$
As $L>0.32$, $5.1<16L$, so $m<19L\le100L$. Hence $\frac1{100}\log\log n\le m\le100\log\log n$. ∎

prompt: We colour all the sides and diagonals of a regular polygon $P$ with $43$ vertices either red or blue in such a way that every vertex is an endpoint of $20$ red segments and $22$ blue segments. A triangle formed by vertices of $P$ is called *monochromatic* if all of its sides have the same colour. Suppose that there are $2022$ blue monochromatic triangles. How many red monochromatic triangles are there?

solutions.title: Double-count cherries
solutions.body:
Call a pair of segments sharing a vertex a *cherry*; it is monochromatic if both segments have the same colour. Every cherry lies in exactly one triangle. A monochromatic triangle contains $3$ monochromatic cherries; any other triangle has two sides of one colour and one of the other, so it contains exactly $1$ monochromatic and $2$ bichromatic cherries.

Let $M$ and $B$ be the numbers of monochromatic and bichromatic cherries. Then each monochromatic triangle contributes $2\cdot3-0=6$ to $2M-B$ and each other triangle contributes $2\cdot1-2=0$, so
$$2M-B=6T,$$
where $T$ is the number of monochromatic triangles.

At each vertex there are $\binom{20}2+\binom{22}2=190+231=421$ monochromatic and $20\cdot22=440$ bichromatic cherries, so $2M-B=43\,(2\cdot421-440)=43\cdot402$. Hence
$$T=\frac{43\cdot402}{6}=43\cdot67=2881,$$
and the number of red monochromatic triangles is $2881-2022=859$.

**Answer: $859$.**

solutions.title: Count non-monochromatic triangles
solutions.body:
There are $\binom{43}3=12341$ triangles. A non-monochromatic triangle has exactly two vertices at which its two sides have different colours (the vertex opposite the odd-coloured side has two equal sides). At each vertex the number of pairs (red segment, blue segment) is $20\cdot22=440$, and each such pair spans exactly one triangle. So
$$\#\{\text{non-monochromatic}\}=\frac{43\cdot440}{2}=9460,$$
the number of monochromatic triangles is $12341-9460=2881$, and the red ones number $2881-2022=859$.

**Answer: $859$.**

prompt:
Let $p>2$ be a prime number. Prove that there is a permutation $(x_1,x_2,\dots,x_{p-1})$ of the numbers $(1,2,\dots,p-1)$ such that
$$x_1x_2+x_2x_3+\dots+x_{p-2}x_{p-1}\equiv2\pmod p .$$
answer: Take $x_i\equiv i^{-1}\pmod p$; then the sum telescopes: $\sum_{i=1}^{p-2}\frac1{i(i+1)}=1-\frac1{p-1}\equiv1+1=2$.

solutions.title: Use inverses: a telescoping sum
solutions.body:
Let $x_i\in\{1,\dots,p-1\}$ be the inverse of $i$ modulo $p$, for $i=1,\dots,p-1$. Inversion is a bijection of the nonzero residues, so $(x_1,\dots,x_{p-1})$ is a permutation of $(1,\dots,p-1)$. Computing modulo $p$,
$$\sum_{i=1}^{p-2}x_ix_{i+1}\equiv\sum_{i=1}^{p-2}\frac1{i(i+1)}=\sum_{i=1}^{p-2}\Big(\frac1i-\frac1{i+1}\Big)=1-\frac1{p-1}\equiv1-\frac1{-1}=2\pmod p .$$
(The partial-fraction identity holds in the field $\mathbb F_p$ because $i,i+1\not\equiv0$ for $1\le i\le p-2$.) ∎

solutions.title: Perturb the identity permutation
solutions.body:
For $p=3$ take $(1,2)$: the sum is $2$. Let $p\ge5$.

The identity permutation gives
$$\sum_{i=1}^{p-2}i(i+1)=\frac{(p-2)(p-1)p}{3}\equiv0\pmod p$$
(as $3\nmid p$, the factor $p$ survives). Replacing a block $(i,i+1,i+2,i+3)$ of consecutive values by $(i,i+2,i+1,i+3)$ changes the three products in it from $i(i+1)+(i+1)(i+2)+(i+2)(i+3)$ to $i(i+2)+(i+2)(i+1)+(i+1)(i+3)$, a **decrease by $3$**. Blocks on disjoint sets of adjacent pairs act independently.

* **$p\equiv2\pmod3$:** swap $3j-1$ and $3j$ for $j=1,\dots,\frac{p-2}3$ (blocks starting at $1,4,7,\dots,p-4$; they use disjoint adjacent pairs). The sum decreases by $3\cdot\frac{p-2}3=p-2$, giving $-(p-2)\equiv2$.
* **$p\equiv1\pmod3$, $p\ge13$:** first replace $(1,2,3,4,5)$ by $(1,4,3,2,5)$: the products $2+6+12+20=40$ become $4+12+6+10=32$, a decrease of $8$. Then swap $3j$ and $3j+1$ for $j=2,\dots,\frac{p-7}3$ (blocks starting at $5,8,\dots,p-8$), each decreasing by $3$, in total $p-10$. The sum becomes $-8-(p-10)\equiv2$.
* **$p=7$:** $(1,4,5,2,3,6)$ gives $4+20+10+6+18=58\equiv2\pmod7$.

In all cases a suitable permutation exists. ∎

prompt:
Let $A_1,A_2,\dots,A_k$ be $n\times n$ idempotent complex matrices such that
$$A_iA_j=-A_jA_i\quad\text{for all }i\ne j.$$
Prove that at least one of the given matrices has rank $\le\frac nk$. (A matrix $A$ is called idempotent if $A^2=A$.)
answer: $\sum A_i$ is again idempotent, and for idempotents rank $=$ trace, so $\sum\operatorname{rank}A_i=\operatorname{tr}\sum A_i=\operatorname{rank}\sum A_i\le n$.

solutions.title: Rank equals trace
solutions.body:
**Lemma.** For an idempotent matrix $B$, $\operatorname{rank}B=\operatorname{tr}B$.

*Proof.* $B$ is annihilated by $x^2-x=x(x-1)$, which has distinct roots, so $B$ is diagonalisable with eigenvalues in $\{0,1\}$. The rank is the number of nonzero eigenvalues (with multiplicity), i.e. the number of eigenvalues equal to $1$, which is the trace. $\square$

**The sum is idempotent.** Let $S=A_1+\dots+A_k$. Then
$$S^2=\sum_iA_i^2+\sum_{i<j}(A_iA_j+A_jA_i)=\sum_iA_i=S .$$
By the lemma (applied to each $A_i$ and to $S$) and linearity of the trace,
$$\sum_{i=1}^k\operatorname{rank}A_i=\sum_{i=1}^k\operatorname{tr}A_i=\operatorname{tr}S=\operatorname{rank}S\le n .$$
Hence the smallest of the $k$ ranks is at most $\frac nk$. ∎

solutions.title: The images form a direct sum
solutions.body:
**Step 1: $A_iA_j=0$ for $i\ne j$.** Let $A=A_i$, $B=A_j$. Using $A^2=A$ and $AB=-BA$ repeatedly:
$$AB=A(AB)=A(-BA)=-(AB)A=(BA)A=BA .$$
Together with $AB=-BA$ this gives $2AB=0$, so $AB=BA=0$.

**Step 2: the images are independent.** Let $V_i=\operatorname{im}A_i$; note $A_iv=v$ for $v\in V_i$ (if $v=A_iw$ then $A_iv=A_i^2w=v$). Suppose $v_1+\dots+v_k=0$ with $v_i\in V_i$. Apply $A_j$: for $i\ne j$, $A_jv_i=A_jA_iw_i=0$, while $A_jv_j=v_j$. So $v_j=0$ for every $j$. Hence the sum $V_1+\dots+V_k$ is direct and
$$\sum_{i=1}^k\operatorname{rank}A_i=\sum_{i=1}^k\dim V_i=\dim(V_1\oplus\dots\oplus V_k)\le n .$$
So some $\operatorname{rank}A_i\le\frac nk$. ∎

prompt: Let $n,k\ge3$ be integers, and let $S$ be a circle. Let $n$ blue points and $k$ red points be chosen uniformly and independently at random on the circle $S$. Denote by $F$ the intersection of the convex hull of the red points and the convex hull of the blue points. Let $m$ be the number of vertices of the convex polygon $F$ (in particular, $m=0$ when $F$ is empty). Find the expected value of $m$.
answer:
$$\mathbb E(m)=\frac{2kn}{n+k-1}-\frac{2\,k!\,n!}{(n+k-1)!}$$
($m$ equals the number of colour changes around the circle, except that it is $0$ instead of $2$ when each colour forms one arc).

solutions.title: Count colour changes around the circle
solutions.body:
**Answer:** $\displaystyle\mathbb E(m)=\frac{2kn}{n+k-1}-\frac{2\,k!\,n!}{(n+k-1)!}$.

With probability $1$ all $n+k$ points are distinct and no three chords through them are concurrent; we assume this. Let $R$ and $B$ be the red and blue convex polygons. Going around the circle, the colours form $2s$ maximal monochromatic runs, alternating red and blue ($s\ge1$); the number of colour changes is $2s$.

**Geometric step: $m=0$ if $s=1$, and $m=2s$ if $s\ge2$.** The edges of $R$ join cyclically consecutive red points $r,r'$. Call such an edge *long* if the arc from $r$ to $r'$ containing no other red point contains blue points (then it contains a whole blue run), and *short* otherwise. There is one long red edge per blue run, i.e. $s$ of them; similarly $s$ long blue edges.

* If $s=1$, the red points fill one arc and the blue points the complementary arc; the line through the long red edge has all red points on one closed side and all blue points strictly on the other side. So $B$ lies in an open half-plane disjoint from the closed half-plane containing $R$, hence $F=\varnothing$ and $m=0$.
* Let $s\ge2$. For a short red edge all blue points lie strictly on one side of its line, the side away from the edge's arc, so this edge does not meet $B$. For a long red edge, its arc contains a blue run and the opposite arc contains another blue run, so its line separates blue points and the chord passes through the interior of $B$; its intersection with $B$ is a non-degenerate segment. The boundary of $F=R\cap B$ consists of the parts of $\partial R$ inside $B$ and of $\partial B$ inside $R$. Each edge line meets the convex set $F$ in at most one segment, so each long edge contributes exactly one side of $F$, short edges none, and different edges lie on different lines. Hence $F$ has $2s$ sides and $m=2s$.

So $m$ equals the number $C$ of colour changes, minus $2$ in the exceptional event $\mathcal E$ that $s=1$.

**Probabilistic step.** Cut the circle at a fixed point and read the colours $C_1,\dots,C_{n+k}$ counterclockwise (cyclically, $C_{n+k}$ is adjacent to $C_1$). All $\binom{n+k}{n}$ colour patterns are equally likely (choose the $n+k$ positions first, then the colours are a uniformly random arrangement). For each of the $n+k$ cyclically adjacent pairs,
$$P(\text{colour change})=\frac{2nk}{(n+k)(n+k-1)},$$
so by linearity $\mathbb E\,C=\frac{2nk}{n+k-1}$. The event $\mathcal E$ consists of the $n+k$ patterns in which the red positions form a cyclic interval (choose where it starts), so
$$P(\mathcal E)=\frac{n+k}{\binom{n+k}{n}}=\frac{n!\,k!}{(n+k-1)!}.$$
Therefore
$$\mathbb E(m)=\mathbb E\,C-2P(\mathcal E)=\frac{2nk}{n+k-1}-\frac{2\,n!\,k!}{(n+k-1)!}.$$
∎
(For example, $n=k=3$ gives $\frac{18}5-\frac{72}{120}=3$.)

solutions.title: Each blue point's outgoing edge
solutions.body:
(Using the geometric description from the first solution: an edge of either polygon contributes one side of $F$ unless all points of the other colour lie on one side of it.)

Label the blue points $A_1,\dots,A_n$. For each $A_i$ let $A_iA'_i$ be the blue edge leaving $A_i$ counterclockwise, and let $b_i=1$ if this edge contains a side of $F$, else $0$; define $r_1,\dots,r_k$ similarly for red points. Then $m=\sum b_i+\sum r_j$.

Read the other $n+k-1$ points counterclockwise from $A_i$; their colour pattern is uniform among the $\binom{n+k-1}{k}$ choices of red positions. The edge $A_iA'_i$ fails to contain a side of $F$ iff all red points are on one side of it, which happens iff either
* the next point after $A_i$ is blue (edge is short): probability $\frac{n-1}{n+k-1}$; or
* the next $k$ points are all red and then come the $n-1$ remaining blue points: probability $1/\binom{n+k-1}{k}$.

(These are exclusive; if the edge spans some but not all red points, red points lie on both sides.) Hence
$$\mathbb E\,b_i=1-\frac{n-1}{n+k-1}-\frac{k!\,(n-1)!}{(n+k-1)!}=\frac{k}{n+k-1}-\frac{k!\,(n-1)!}{(n+k-1)!},$$
and symmetrically $\mathbb E\,r_j=\frac{n}{n+k-1}-\frac{n!\,(k-1)!}{(n+k-1)!}$. Summing,
$$\mathbb E(m)=n\,\mathbb E b_1+k\,\mathbb E r_1=\frac{2nk}{n+k-1}-\frac{2\,n!\,k!}{(n+k-1)!}.$$
∎
